questions.question: An electron is projected with uniform velocity along the axis inside a current carrying long solenoid. Then -
options: The electron will continue to move with uniform velocity along the axis of the solenoid
the electron will be accelerated along the axis
the electron path will be circular about the axis
the electron will experience a force at 45° to the axis and execute a helical path.
questions.explanation:
### Understanding the magnetic force on a charged particle

The magnetic force \(\vec{F}\) on a charged particle with charge \(q\) moving with velocity \(\vec{V}\) in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) is given by the Lorentz force formula:
\vec{F} = q(\vec{V} \times \vec{B})
Inside a long current-carrying solenoid, the magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) is uniform and directed along the axis of the solenoid. The electron is projected with uniform velocity \(\vec{V}\) along the axis of the solenoid.
Therefore, the velocity vector \(\vec{V}\) and the magnetic field vector \(\vec{B}\) are in the same direction (or anti-parallel, depending on the direction of current and electron projection, but in either case, they are parallel).
When two vectors are parallel, their cross product is zero. Thus, \(\vec{V} \times \vec{B} = 0\).
Consequently, the force on the electron will be zero:
\vec{F} = q(0) = 0

### Conclusion on electron's motion

Since there is no net force acting on the electron, according to Newton's first law of motion, the electron will continue to move with its initial uniform velocity along the axis of the solenoid.
Option 1 is correct.

questions.question: A particle of charge \(1.6\,\mu C\) and mass \(16\,\mu g\) is present in a strong magnetic field of \(6.28\,T\). The particle is then fired perpendicular to magnetic field. The time required for the particle to return to original location for the first time is ______ s. (\(\pi = 3.14\))

Uniform magnetic fields of different strengths (\(B_1\) and \(B_2\)), both normal to the plane of the paper exist as shown in the figure. A charged particle of mass \(m\) and charge \(q\), at the interface at an instant, moves into the region 2 with velocity \(v\) and returns to the interface. It continues to move into region 1 and finally reaches the interface. What is the displacement of the particle during this movement along the interface ?
(Consider the velocity of the particle to be normal to the magnetic field and \(B_2 > B_1\))
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Understanding the motion of the charged particle

As \(\vec{v}\) is \(\perp\) to \(\vec{B}\), the charged particle will move in a circular path. The radius of this circular path is given by:
R = \frac{mv}{qB}

### Step 2: Calculating displacement in each region

From the diagram, the particle starts at point A and ends at point C. The net displacement is AC.
The particle first moves into region 2 (magnetic field \(B_2\)) from A, completing a semi-circular path and returning to the interface at point D. The diameter of this semi-circle is \(2R_2 = \frac{2mv}{qB_2}\). So, the displacement along the interface in region 2 is AD.
Then, the particle moves into region 1 (magnetic field \(B_1\)) from D, completing another semi-circular path and returning to the interface at point C. The diameter of this semi-circle is \(2R_1 = \frac{2mv}{qB_1}\). So, the displacement along the interface in region 1 is CD.
The net displacement AC is the difference between the displacement in region 1 (CD) and the displacement in region 2 (AD), as they are in opposite directions along the interface from the perspective of the starting point A.
AC = CD - AD
AC = \frac{2mv}{qB_1} - \frac{2mv}{qB_2}

### Step 3: Final displacement calculation

Factor out the common terms:
AC = \frac{2mv}{q} \left(\frac{1}{B_1} - \frac{1}{B_2}\right)
Combine the terms in the parenthesis:
AC = \frac{2mv}{q} \left(\frac{B_2 - B_1}{B_1 B_2}\right)
Rearranging to match the options:
AC = \frac{2mv}{qB_1} \left(\frac{B_2 - B_1}{B_2}\right)
AC = \frac{2mv}{qB_1} \left(1 - \frac{B_1}{B_2}\right)
The final displacement of the particle along the interface is \(\frac{2mv}{qB_1} \left[1 - \frac{B_1}{B_2}\right]\).

The force per unit length experienced by the conductor is __________ \(10^{-6}\) N/m.
A 4.0 cm long straight wire carrying a current of 8A is placed perpendicular to an uniform magnetic field of strength 0.15 T. The magnetic force on the wire is ________ mN.
questions.explanation:
Given:
• Length of wire \(l = 4.0\) cm \(= 4.0 \times 10^{-2}\) m
• Current \(I = 8\) A
• Magnetic field strength \(B = 0.15\) T
• Wire is placed perpendicular, so \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\)

### Step 1: Apply the formula for magnetic force on a current-carrying wire

The magnetic force \(F\) on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field is given by:
F = I l B \sin \theta

### Step 2: Substitute the given values and calculate the force

Since the wire is perpendicular to the magnetic field, \(\sin \theta = \sin 90^{\circ} = 1\).
F = 8 \times (4.0 \times 10^{-2}) \times 0.15 \times 1
F = 8 \times \frac{4}{100} \times 0.15
F = 0.048 \text{ N}

### Step 3: Convert the force to milliNewtons (mN)

Since \(1\) N \(= 1000\) mN:
F = 0.048 \times 1000 \text{ mN}
F = 48 \text{ mN}

questions.question: The magnetic moments associated with two closely wound circular coils A and B of radius \(r_{A} = 10\) cm and \(r_{B} = 20\) cm respectively are equal if : (Where \(N_{A}, I_{A}\) and \(N_{B}, I_{B}\) are number of turn and current of A and B respectively)
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution


### Step 1: Formula for Magnetic Moment

The magnetic moment \(m\) of a circular coil is given by:
m = IAN
Where \(I\) is the current, \(A\) is the area of the coil, and \(N\) is the number of turns.

### Step 2: Magnetic moment of coil A

For coil A, with radius \(r_{A} = 10\) cm, current \(I_{A}\), and number of turns \(N_{A}\):
m_{A} = I_{A} \pi r_{A}^2 N_{A}
m_{A} = I_{A} \pi N_{A} (10)^2
m_{A} = 100 \pi I_{A} N_{A} \quad \ldots(1)

### Step 3: Magnetic moment of coil B

For coil B, with radius \(r_{B} = 20\) cm, current \(I_{B}\), and number of turns \(N_{B}\):
m_{B} = I_{B} N_{B} \pi r_{B}^2
m_{B} = I_{B} N_{B} \pi (20)^2
m_{B} = 400 \pi I_{B} N_{B} \quad \ldots(2)

### Step 4: Equate magnetic moments

Given that the magnetic moments are equal, \(m_{A} = m_{B}\):
100 \pi I_{A} N_{A} = 400 \pi I_{B} N_{B}
Divide both sides by \(100 \pi\):
I_{A} N_{A} = 4 I_{B} N_{B}
This matches option (3).

A 5 mg particle carrying a charge of \(5\pi \times 10^{-6}\) C is moving with velocity of \((3\hat{i} + 2\hat{k}) \times 10^{-2}\) m/s in a region having magnetic field \(\vec{B} = 0.1 \hat{k}\) Wb/m\(^{2}\). It moves a distance of \(\alpha\) meter along \(\hat{k}\) when it completes 5 revolutions. The value of \(\alpha\) is ________.
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution


### Step 1: Identify the given parameters and velocity components

Given:
• Mass of the particle, \(m = 5 \text{ mg} = 5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ kg}\)
• Charge of the particle, \(q = 5\pi \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}\)
• Velocity of the particle, \(\vec{v} = (3\hat{i} + 2\hat{k}) \times 10^{-2}\text{ m/s}\)
• Magnetic field, \(\vec{B} = 0.1 \hat{k}\text{ Wb/m}^2\)
The velocity vector can be decomposed into components parallel and perpendicular to the magnetic field \(\vec{B}\). Since \(\vec{B}\) is along the \(\hat{k}\) direction:
• Velocity component parallel to \(\vec{B}\): \(v_{\parallel} = 2 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m/s}\)
• Velocity component perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\): \(v_{\perp} = 3 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m/s}\)

### Step 2: Calculate the time period of one revolution

The time period \(T\) for one complete revolution of a charged particle in a magnetic field is given by:
T = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}
Substitute the given values:
T = \frac{2\pi (5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ kg})}{(5\pi \times 10^{-6}\text{ C})(0.1\text{ T})}
T = \frac{2\pi \times 5 \times 10^{-6}}{0.5\pi \times 10^{-6}}
T = \frac{10\pi \times 10^{-6}}{0.5\pi \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{10}{0.5} = 20\text{ s}

### Step 3: Calculate the distance moved along \(\hat{k}\) in 5 revolutions

The particle moves along the \(\hat{k}\) direction due to the parallel component of velocity \(v_{\parallel}\). The distance covered in one revolution along the \(\hat{k}\) direction is:
d_{\text{one revolution}} = v_{\parallel} \times T
d_{\text{one revolution}} = (2 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m/s}) \times (20\text{ s}) = 0.4\text{ m}
For 5 revolutions, the total distance \(\alpha\) moved along the \(\hat{k}\) direction is:
\alpha = 5 \times d_{\text{one revolution}}
\alpha = 5 \times 0.4\text{ m} = 2\text{ m}

questions.question: A particle having charge \(10^{-9}\) C moving in x-y plane in fields of \(0.4 \hat{j}\) N/C and \(4 \times 10^{-3} \hat{k}\) T experiences a force of \((4\hat{i}+2\hat{j}) \times 10^{-10}\) N. The velocity of the particle at that instant is ______ m/s.
questions.explanation:
\vec{F} = q\vec{E} + q(\vec{V} \times \vec{B})
(4\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}) \times 10^{-10} = 10^{-9}[0.4 \hat{j} + (v_x \hat{i} + v_y \hat{j}) \times (4 \times 10^{-3}) \hat{k}]
(4\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}) \times 10^{-10} = 10^{-9} (0.4 \hat{j} + v_x (4 \times 10^{-3}) (\hat{i} \times \hat{k}) + v_y (4 \times 10^{-3}) (\hat{j} \times \hat{k}))
(4\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}) \times 10^{-10} = 10^{-9} (0.4 \hat{j} + v_x (4 \times 10^{-3}) (-\hat{j}) + v_y (4 \times 10^{-3}) (\hat{i}))
(4\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}) \times 10^{-10} = 10^{-9} (0.4 \hat{j} - 4 \times 10^{-3} v_x \hat{j} + 4 \times 10^{-3} v_y \hat{i})
On comparing the coefficients of \(\hat{i}\) and \(\hat{j}\) on both sides:
\text{For } \hat{i}: 4 \times 10^{-10} = 10^{-9} (4 \times 10^{-3} v_y)
4 \times 10^{-10} = 4 \times 10^{-12} v_y
v_y = \frac{4 \times 10^{-10}}{4 \times 10^{-12}} = 10^2 = 100
\text{For } \hat{j}: 2 \times 10^{-10} = 10^{-9} (0.4 - 4 \times 10^{-3} v_x)
2 \times 10^{-10} = 0.4 \times 10^{-9} - 4 \times 10^{-12} v_x
2 \times 10^{-10} = 4 \times 10^{-10} - 4 \times 10^{-12} v_x
4 \times 10^{-12} v_x = 4 \times 10^{-10} - 2 \times 10^{-10}
4 \times 10^{-12} v_x = 2 \times 10^{-10}
v_x = \frac{2 \times 10^{-10}}{4 \times 10^{-12}} = 0.5 \times 10^2 = 50
Thus, we have \(v_y = 100\) m/s and \(v_x = 50\) m/s.
The velocity vector is:
\vec{V} = v_x \hat{i} + v_y \hat{j} = 50\hat{i} + 100\hat{j}

The number of turns of the coil of a moving coil galvanometer is increased in order to increase current sensitivity by 50%. The percentage change in voltage sensitivity of the galvanometer will be :
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Understand the definitions of current and voltage sensitivity

The current sensitivity (\(\alpha_I\)) of a moving coil galvanometer is given by:
\alpha_I = \frac{NAB}{K}
Where N is the number of turns, A is the area of the coil, B is the magnetic field strength, and K is the torsional constant of the suspension wire.
The voltage sensitivity (\(\alpha_v\)) is given by:
\alpha_v = \frac{NAB}{KR}
Where R is the resistance of the galvanometer coil.

### Step 2: Relate current and voltage sensitivity

From the above definitions, we can express voltage sensitivity in terms of current sensitivity:
\alpha_v = \frac{\alpha_I}{R}

### Step 3: Analyze the effect of increasing current sensitivity by 50%

Given that the current sensitivity \(\alpha_I\) is increased by 50%. This means the new current sensitivity \(\alpha_I'\) is:
\alpha_I' = \alpha_I + 0.5\alpha_I = 1.5\alpha_I
Since \(\alpha_I = \frac{NAB}{K}\), and A, B, K are constants for a given galvanometer, for \(\alpha_I\) to increase by 50%, the number of turns N must increase by 50%. So, the new number of turns \(N' = 1.5N\).

### Step 4: Determine the change in resistance R

The resistance R of the coil is directly proportional to the length of the wire, which in turn is directly proportional to the number of turns N (assuming the wire material and cross-sectional area remain constant).
Therefore, if N increases by 50%, the resistance R will also increase by 50%. So, the new resistance \(R' = 1.5R\).

### Step 5: Calculate the new voltage sensitivity

Using the relationship \(\alpha_v = \frac{\alpha_I}{R}\), the new voltage sensitivity \(\alpha_v'\) will be:
\alpha_v' = \frac{\alpha_I'}{R'} = \frac{1.5\alpha_I}{1.5R} = \frac{\alpha_I}{R}
Thus, we find that \(\alpha_v' = \alpha_v\). The voltage sensitivity remains unchanged.

### Step 6: Calculate the percentage change in voltage sensitivity

The percentage change in voltage sensitivity is given by:
\text{Percentage Change} = \frac{\alpha_v' - \alpha_v}{\alpha_v} \times 100\% = \frac{\alpha_v - \alpha_v}{\alpha_v} \times 100\% = 0\%

questions.question: A particle of charge \(q\) and mass \(m\) is projected from origin with an initial velocity \(\vec{v} = \left(\frac{v_0}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{x} + \frac{v_0}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{y}\right)\). There exists a uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B} = B_0\hat{z}\) and a space varying electric field \(\vec{E} = E_0e^{-\lambda x}\hat{x}\) within the region \(0 \le x \le L\). After travelling a distance such that x-coordinate has changed from \(x = 0\) to \(x = L\), the change in the kinetic energy is \(\underline{\hspace{4cm}}\) .
questions.explanation:
The change in kinetic energy is equal to the total work done on the particle. The work done by the magnetic field is always zero because the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity, so \(W_m = 0\).
Therefore, the change in kinetic energy \(\Delta K\) is solely due to the work done by the electric field \(W_e\).
\Delta K = W_e + W_m = W_e + 0
The work done by the electric field is given by the integral of the electric force over the displacement. The electric force is \(\vec{F}_e = q\vec{E}\).
\Delta K = \int_{0}^{L} \vec{F}_e \cdot d\vec{x} = \int_{0}^{L} q\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{x}
Given electric field is \(\vec{E} = E_0e^{-\lambda x}\hat{x}\). The displacement is along the x-axis, so \(d\vec{x} = dx\hat{x}\).
\Delta K = \int_{0}^{L} q(E_0e^{-\lambda x}\hat{x}) \cdot (dx\hat{x})
\Delta K = qE_0 \int_{0}^{L} e^{-\lambda x} dx
Now, we evaluate the integral:
\Delta K = qE_0 \left[ \frac{e^{-\lambda x}}{-\lambda} \right]_{0}^{L}
\Delta K = \frac{qE_0}{-\lambda} (e^{-\lambda L} - e^0)
\Delta K = \frac{qE_0}{-\lambda} (e^{-\lambda L} - 1)
\Delta K = \frac{qE_0}{\lambda} (1 - e^{-\lambda L})

questions.question: A charge particle of \(2\mu\text{C}\) accelerated by a potential difference of 100 V enters a region of uniform magnetic field of magnitude \(4\text{mT}\) at right angle to the direction of field. The charge particle completes semicircle of radius \(3\text{ cm}\) inside magnetic field. The mass of the charge particle is __________ \(\times 10^{-18}\) kg.

A particle of charge \(q\), mass \(m\) and kinetic energy \(E\) enters in magnetic field perpendicular to its velocity and undergoes a circular arc of radius \(r\). Which of the following curves represents the variation of \(r\) with \(E\)?
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Relate magnetic force to centripetal force

When a charged particle moves perpendicular to a magnetic field, the magnetic force provides the necessary centripetal force for circular motion.
\frac{mv^2}{r} = qvB

### Step 2: Express velocity in terms of radius

From the force balance equation, we can simplify to find the velocity \(v\):
mv = qBr \implies v = \frac{qBr}{m}

### Step 3: Relate kinetic energy to velocity

The kinetic energy \(E\) of the particle is given by:
E = \frac{1}{2}mv^2

### Step 4: Substitute velocity into kinetic energy equation

Substitute the expression for \(v\) from Step 2 into the kinetic energy equation:
E = \frac{1}{2}m\left(\frac{qBr}{m}\right)^2
E = \frac{1}{2}m\left(\frac{q^2B^2r^2}{m^2}\right)
E = \frac{q^2B^2r^2}{2m}

### Step 5: Determine the relationship between r and E

Rearranging the equation to show the dependence of \(E\) on \(r\):
E = \left(\frac{q^2B^2}{2m}\right)r^2
Since \(q\), \(B\), and \(m\) are constants, we can say:
E \propto r^2
This implies that \(r \propto \sqrt{E}\). A graph of \(r\) versus \(E\) will show \(r\) increasing with \(E\) but with a decreasing slope, characteristic of a square root function.
This corresponds to curve (4).
The final answer is D.

### Detailed Solution


### Step 1: Understand the relationship between magnetic force, velocity, and magnetic field.

The magnetic force \(\vec{F}_{B}\) on a charged particle moving in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) with velocity \(\vec{V}\) is given by \(\vec{F}_{B} = q(\vec{V} \times \vec{B})\). This implies that the magnetic force is always perpendicular to both the velocity vector and the magnetic field vector.
\vec{F}_{B} \propto (\vec{V} \times \vec{B}) \implies \vec{F}_{B} \perp \vec{B}

### Step 2: Relate acceleration to magnetic force and magnetic field.

Since \(\vec{F}_{B} = m\vec{a}\) (where m is the mass of the particle and \(\vec{a}\) is its acceleration), the acceleration \(\vec{a}\) must also be perpendicular to the magnetic field \(\vec{B}\).
\vec{a} \perp \vec{B}

### Step 3: Apply the condition for perpendicular vectors.

If two vectors are perpendicular, their dot product is zero. So, \(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{B} = 0\).

### Step 4: Substitute the given vectors and solve for x.

Given magnetic field \(\vec{B} = (3\hat{i}+2\hat{j})\)T and acceleration \(\vec{a} = (4\hat{i}-\frac{x}{2}\hat{j})\) m/s\(^2\).
\vec{a} \cdot \vec{B} = (4\hat{i}-\frac{x}{2}\hat{j}) \cdot (3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}) = 0
(4)(3) + (-\frac{x}{2})(2) = 0
12 - x = 0
x = 12

questions.question:
A circular coil of radius 2 cm and 125 turns carries a current of 1 A. The coil is placed in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude 0.4 T. The axis of the coil makes an angle of 30° with the direction of the magnetic field. The torque acting on the coil is \(\alpha \times 10^{-4}\) N.m. The value of \(\alpha\) is __________.
(\(\pi = 3.14\))
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Identify the given values and formula for torque.

Given values are:
• Radius of coil, \(r = 2\) cm \(= 0.02\) m
• Number of turns, \(N = 125\)
• Current, \(I = 1\) A
• Magnetic field, \(B = 0.4\) T
• Angle between axis of coil and magnetic field, \(\theta = 30^\circ\)
• Torque, \(\tau = \alpha \times 10^{-4}\) N.m
The formula for torque acting on a current loop in a magnetic field is:
\tau = |\vec{M} \times \vec{B}|
Where \(\vec{M}\) is the magnetic moment of the coil, given by \(\vec{M} = NIA\vec{n}\), where \(A\) is the area of the coil and \(\vec{n}\) is the unit vector normal to the plane of the coil (along the axis).
\tau = NIAB \sin\theta

### Step 2: Calculate the area of the coil.

The area of the circular coil is \(A = \pi r^2\).
A = \pi (0.02 \text{ m})^2 = \pi (4 \times 10^{-4}) \text{ m}^2

### Step 3: Substitute the values into the torque formula.

\tau = 125 \times 1 \text{ A} \times \pi (4 \times 10^{-4}) \text{ m}^2 \times 0.4 \text{ T} \times \sin(30^\circ)
\tau = 125 \times \pi \times 4 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.4 \times \frac{1}{2}
\tau = 125 \times \pi \times 4 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.2
\tau = 500 \times \pi \times 10^{-4} \times 0.2
\tau = 100 \pi \times 10^{-4} \text{ N.m}

### Step 4: Determine the value of \(\alpha\).

We are given that the torque is \(\tau = \alpha \times 10^{-4}\) N.m.
Comparing this with our calculated value:
\alpha \times 10^{-4} = 100 \pi \times 10^{-4}
\alpha = 100 \pi
Using \(\pi = 3.14\):
\alpha = 100 \times 3.14 = 314

questions.question: A bar magnet with a magnetic moment \(5.0 \text{Am}^2\) is placed in parallel position relative to a magnetic field of \(0.4 \text{ T}\). The amount of required work done in turning the magnet from parallel to antiparallel position relative to the field direction is ________.
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution


### Step 1: Identify the given values and formula for work done

Given:
• Magnetic moment, \(M = 5.0 \text{ Am}^2\)
• Magnetic field, \(B = 0.4 \text{ T}\)
The work done in rotating a magnetic dipole in a magnetic field is given by:
W = MB(\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2)

### Step 2: Determine initial and final angles

• Initial position: parallel to the field direction, so \(\theta_1 = 0^\circ\)
• Final position: antiparallel to the field direction, so \(\theta_2 = 180^\circ\)

### Step 3: Substitute values into the formula and calculate work done

W = MB(\cos 0^\circ - \cos 180^\circ)
We know that \(\cos 0^\circ = 1\) and \(\cos 180^\circ = -1\).
W = MB(1 - (-1))
W = MB(2)
W = 2MB
Now, substitute the given values of M and B:
W = 2 \times 5.0 \times 0.4
W = 10 \times 0.4
W = 4 \text{ J}
Thus, the required work done is \(4 \text{ J}\).

questions.question:
Given below are two statements :
Statements I : If the number of turns in the coil of a moving coil galvanometer is doubled then the current sensitivity becomes double.
Statements II : Increasing current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer by only increasing the number of turns in the coil will also increase its voltage sensitivity in the same ratio.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution


### Step 1: Analyze Statement I (Current Sensitivity)

The current sensitivity (C.S.) of a moving coil galvanometer is defined as the deflection per unit current. It is given by the formula:
C.S. = \frac{\theta}{I} = \frac{NBA}{K}
Where N is the number of turns in the coil, B is the magnetic field strength, A is the area of the coil, and K is the torsional constant of the suspension wire.
If the number of turns N is doubled (N \(\to\) 2N), the new current sensitivity (C.S.') will be:
C.S.' = \frac{(2N)BA}{K} = 2 \left(\frac{NBA}{K}\right) = 2 \cdot C.S.
Thus, if the number of turns is doubled, the current sensitivity becomes double. So, Statement I is TRUE.

### Step 2: Analyze Statement II (Voltage Sensitivity)

The voltage sensitivity (V.S.) of a moving coil galvanometer is defined as the deflection per unit voltage. It is given by the formula:
V.S. = \frac{\theta}{V}
Since V = IR (where I is current and R is the resistance of the coil), we can write:
V.S. = \frac{\theta}{IR}
We know that \(\frac{\theta}{I} = C.S. = \frac{NBA}{K}\). Substituting this into the V.S. equation:
V.S. = \frac{C.S.}{R} = \frac{NBA}{KR}
When the number of turns N in the coil is increased, the length of the wire used to make the coil increases, and consequently, the resistance R of the coil also increases proportionally. So, if N \(\to\) 2N, then R \(\to\) 2R.
Now, let's find the new voltage sensitivity (V.S.') when N \(\to\) 2N and R \(\to\) 2R:
V.S.' = \frac{(2N)BA}{K(2R)} = \frac{NBA}{KR} = V.S.
Therefore, increasing current sensitivity by only increasing the number of turns in the coil does NOT increase its voltage sensitivity in the same ratio; it remains constant. So, Statement II is FALSE.

### Step 3: Conclusion

Based on the analysis, Statement I is true, and Statement II is false.

questions.question: An insulated wire is wound so that it forms a flat coil with \(N = 200\) turns. The radius of the innermost turn is \(r_{1} = 3\) cm, and of the outermost turn \(r_{2} = 6\) cm. If \(20\) mA current flow in it then the magnetic moment will be \(\alpha \times 10^{-2}\) A.m\(^{2}\). The value of \(\alpha\) is ________.
questions.explanation:
### Calculation of Magnetic Moment for a Flat Coil


### Step 1: Visualize the coil and define parameters

The problem describes a flat coil with \(N\) turns, an innermost radius \(r_{1}\) and an outermost radius \(r_{2}\). A current \(I\) flows through it. We need to find the magnetic moment \(M\).

### Step 2: Derive the differential magnetic moment

Consider a differential ring of radius \(r\) and thickness \(dr\). The number of turns in this differential ring is \(dN\). The total number of turns \(N\) is distributed uniformly over the radial width \((r_{ext} - r_{i})\). Therefore, the number of turns per unit length is \(\frac{N}{r_{ext} - r_{i}}\). So, \(dN = \frac{N}{r_{ext} - r_{i}} dr\).
The magnetic moment of a single turn is \(I \times A\), where \(A = \pi r^2\) is the area. For \(dN\) turns, the differential magnetic moment \(dM\) is:
dM = (I \cdot dN) \pi r^2
dM = I \left( \frac{N}{r_{ext} - r_{i}} dr \right) \pi r^2

### Step 3: Integrate to find the total magnetic moment

To find the total magnetic moment \(M\), we integrate \(dM\) from the innermost radius \(r_{i}\) to the outermost radius \(r_{ext}\):
M = \int_{r_{i}}^{r_{ext}} I \frac{N}{r_{ext} - r_{i}} \pi r^2 dr
M = \frac{I \pi N}{r_{ext} - r_{i}} \int_{r_{i}}^{r_{ext}} r^2 dr
M = \frac{I \pi N}{r_{ext} - r_{i}} \left[ \frac{r^3}{3} \right]_{r_{i}}^{r_{ext}}
M = \frac{I \pi N}{3(r_{ext} - r_{i})} (r_{ext}^3 - r_{i}^3)

### Step 4: Substitute the given values

Given values:
• Number of turns, \(N = 200\)
• Innermost radius, \(r_{i} = 3\) cm \(= 3 \times 10^{-2}\) m
• Outermost radius, \(r_{ext} = 6\) cm \(= 6 \times 10^{-2}\) m
• Current, \(I = 20\) mA \(= 20 \times 10^{-3}\) A
M = \frac{(20 \times 10^{-3}) \times \pi \times 200}{3(6 \times 10^{-2} - 3 \times 10^{-2})} ((6 \times 10^{-2})^3 - (3 \times 10^{-2})^3)
M = \frac{20 \times 10^{-3} \times 3.14 \times 200}{3(3 \times 10^{-2})} (216 \times 10^{-6} - 27 \times 10^{-6})
M = \frac{12560 \times 10^{-3}}{9 \times 10^{-2}} (189 \times 10^{-6})
M = \frac{2512 \times 10^{-3}}{9 \times 10^{-2}} (189 \times 10^{-6})
M = \frac{2373.84 \times 10^{-6}}{9 \times 10^{-2}}
M = 263.76 \times 10^{-4} \text{ A.m}^2
M = 2.6376 \times 10^{-2} \text{ A.m}^2

### Step 5: Determine the value of \(\alpha\)

The magnetic moment is given as \(\alpha \times 10^{-2}\) A.m\(^{2}\). Comparing this with our calculated value:
\alpha \times 10^{-2} = 2.6376 \times 10^{-2}
\alpha \approx 2.64
The value of \(\alpha\) is approximately 2.64.

questions.question: A current carrying circular loop of radius 2 cm with unit normal \(\hat{n} = \frac{\hat{k} + \hat{i}}{\sqrt{2}}\) is placed in a magnetic field, \(\vec{B} = B_0(3\hat{i} + 2\hat{k})\). If \(B_0 = 4 \times 10^{-3}\) T and current \(I=100\sqrt{2}\) A, the torque experienced by the loop is __________ Wb.A. (\(\pi = 3.14\))
questions.explanation:
Given values are:
• Radius of the circular loop, \(r = 2\) cm \(= 0.02\) m
• Unit normal vector, \(\hat{n} = \frac{\hat{k} + \hat{i}}{\sqrt{2}}\) 
• Magnetic field, \(\vec{B} = B_0(3\hat{i} + 2\hat{k})\)
• \(B_0 = 4 \times 10^{-3}\) T
• Current, \(I = 100\sqrt{2}\) A
• \(\pi = 3.14\)
The formula for torque experienced by a current loop in a magnetic field is \(\vec{\tau} = \vec{M} \times \vec{B}\), where \(\vec{M}\) is the magnetic moment.
The magnetic moment \(\vec{M}\) is given by \(\vec{M} = I A \hat{n}\), where \(A\) is the area of the loop.
A = \pi r^2 = 3.14 \times (0.02)^2 = 3.14 \times 4 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2
\vec{M} = I A \hat{n} = (100\sqrt{2}) \times (3.14 \times 4 \times 10^{-4}) \times \left(\frac{\hat{k} + \hat{i}}{\sqrt{2}}\right)
\vec{M} = 100 \times 3.14 \times 4 \times 10^{-4} (\hat{k} + \hat{i})
\vec{M} = 1256 \times 10^{-4} (\hat{k} + \hat{i}) \text{ A m}^2
Now, substitute \(\vec{M}\) and \(\vec{B}\) into the torque formula:
\vec{\tau} = \vec{M} \times \vec{B}
\vec{\tau} = [100 \times 3.14 \times 4 \times 10^{-4} (\hat{k} + \hat{i})] \times [B_0(3\hat{i} + 2\hat{k})]
\vec{\tau} = (100 \times 3.14 \times 4 \times 10^{-4} \times B_0) [(\hat{k} + \hat{i}) \times (3\hat{i} + 2\hat{k})]
Substitute \(B_0 = 4 \times 10^{-3}\) T:
\vec{\tau} = (100 \times 3.14 \times 4 \times 10^{-4} \times 4 \times 10^{-3}) [(\hat{k} + \hat{i}) \times (3\hat{i} + 2\hat{k})]
\vec{\tau} = (5024 \times 10^{-7}) [(\hat{k} + \hat{i}) \times (3\hat{i} + 2\hat{k})]
Calculate the cross product:
(\hat{k} + \hat{i}) \times (3\hat{i} + 2\hat{k}) = (\hat{k} \times 3\hat{i}) + (\hat{k} \times 2\hat{k}) + (\hat{i} \times 3\hat{i}) + (\hat{i} \times 2\hat{k})
= 3(\hat{k} \times \hat{i}) + 0 + 0 + 2(\hat{i} \times \hat{k})
= 3\hat{j} + 2(-\hat{j})
= 3\hat{j} - 2\hat{j} = \hat{j}
Therefore, the torque is:
\vec{\tau} = (5024 \times 10^{-7}) \hat{j} \text{ Wb.A}
This can also be written as:
\vec{\tau} = 50.24 \times 10^{-5} \hat{j} \text{ Wb.A}

questions.question:
A proton moving with a constant velocity passes through a region of space without any change in its velocity. If \(\vec{E}\) and \(\vec{B}\) represent the electric and magnetic fields respectively, then the region of space may have :
(A) \(E = 0, B = 0\)
(B) \(E = 0, B \neq 0\)
(C) \(E \neq 0, B = 0\)
(D) \(E \neq 0, B \neq 0\)
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below ;
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

For a proton moving with constant velocity, the net force acting on it must be zero. The electric force \(\vec{F}_E\) and magnetic force \(\vec{F}_B\) are given by:
\vec{F}_E = q\vec{E}
\vec{F}_B = q(\vec{V} \times \vec{B})
For zero net force, \(\vec{F}_E + \vec{F}_B = 0\), which implies \(q\vec{E} + q(\vec{V} \times \vec{B}) = 0\), or \(\vec{E} = -(\vec{V} \times \vec{B})\).
Let's analyze each case:
(A) \(E = 0, B = 0\): If both fields are zero, then \(0 = -(\vec{V} \times \vec{0})\), which is \(0 = 0\). No forces act, so velocity remains constant. This case is possible.
(B) \(E = 0, B \neq 0\): If \(E = 0\), then \(0 = -(\vec{V} \times \vec{B})\). This implies \(\vec{V} \times \vec{B} = 0\), which means \(\vec{V}\) is parallel or anti-parallel to \(\vec{B}\). In this situation, the magnetic force is zero, and since \(E=0\), the electric force is also zero. Thus, the net force is zero. This case is possible.
(C) \(E \neq 0, B = 0\): If \(B = 0\), then \(\vec{E} = -(\vec{V} \times \vec{0})\), which means \(\vec{E} = 0\). This contradicts the condition \(E \neq 0\). If \(E \neq 0\) and \(B = 0\), there would be a net electric force \(q\vec{E}\) acting on the proton, changing its velocity. This case is NOT possible.
(D) \(E \neq 0, B \neq 0\): This case is possible if \(\vec{E}\) is perpendicular to both \(\vec{V}\) and \(\vec{B}\), and \(E = VB\) (velocity selector condition). In this scenario, the electric force \(q\vec{E}\) and magnetic force \(q(\vec{V} \times \vec{B})\) are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, resulting in zero net force. This case is possible.
Therefore, the possible scenarios are (A), (B), and (D).
Comparing with the given options, option (3) which states "(A), (B) and (D) only" is correct.

questions.question: A short bar magnet placed with its axis at 30° with an external field of 800 Gauss, experiences a torque of 0.016 N.m. The work done in moving it from most stable to most unstable position is \(\alpha \times 10^{-3}\) J. The value of \(\alpha\) is _______.
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Calculate magnetic dipole moment (\(\mu\))

The torque \(\tau\) experienced by a bar magnet in an external magnetic field \(B\) is given by \(\tau = \mu B \sin \theta\).
Given: \(\tau = 0.016\) N.m, \(\theta = 30^\circ\), \(\sin 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2}\).
0.016 = \mu \times B \times \frac{1}{2}
\implies \mu = \frac{0.016 \times 2}{B} = \frac{0.032}{B}

### Step 2: Calculate work done (\(W_{\text{ext}}\))

The potential energy of a magnetic dipole in a magnetic field is \(U = -\mu B \cos \theta\).
Most stable position: \(\theta_i = 0^\circ\), so \(U_i = -\mu B \cos 0^\circ = -\mu B\).
Most unstable position: \(\theta_f = 180^\circ\), so \(U_f = -\mu B \cos 180^\circ = -\mu B (-1) = \mu B\).
The work done in moving the magnet from the most stable to the most unstable position is the change in potential energy:
W_{\text{ext}} = U_f - U_i = \mu B - (-\mu B) = 2\mu B
Substitute the expression for \(\mu\) from Step 1:
W_{\text{ext}} = 2 \times \left(\frac{0.032}{B}\right) \times B
W_{\text{ext}} = 2 \times 0.032 = 0.064 \text{ J}

### Step 3: Determine the value of \(\alpha\)

The problem states that the work done is \(\alpha \times 10^{-3}\) J.
0.064 = \alpha \times 10^{-3}
\alpha = \frac{0.064}{10^{-3}} = 0.064 \times 10^3
\alpha = 64

questions.question: A uniform magnetic field of \(2\times 10^{-3}\)T acts along positive Y-direction. A rectangular loop of sides 20 cm and 10 cm with current of 5A is in Y-Z plane. The current is in anticlockwise sense with reference to negative X axis. Magnitude and direction of the torque is:
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Determine the magnetic moment \(\vec{M}\) of the loop.

The magnetic moment \(\vec{M}\) of a current loop is given by \(\vec{M} = i\vec{A}\), where \(i\) is the current and \(\vec{A}\) is the area vector. The magnitude of the area is \(A = \text{length} \times \text{width} = 20 \text{ cm} \times 10 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m} \times 0.1 \text{ m} = 0.02 \text{ m}^2\).
The loop is in the Y-Z plane. The current is in an anticlockwise sense with reference to the negative X-axis. This means if you look from the negative X-axis towards the origin, the current is anticlockwise. Therefore, the area vector \(\vec{A}\) points in the negative X-direction (by the right-hand rule).
\vec{M} = i\vec{A}
= 5 \times (0.2 \times 0.1) (-\hat{i})
= 0.1(-\hat{i}) \text{ A} \cdot \text{m}^2

### Step 2: Determine the torque \(\vec{\tau}\) on the loop.

The torque \(\vec{\tau}\) on a current loop in a magnetic field is given by \(\vec{\tau} = \vec{M} \times \vec{B}\).
The magnetic field is given as \(2\times 10^{-3}\)T along the positive Y-direction, so \(\vec{B} = 2\times 10^{-3} \hat{j}\) T.
\vec{\tau} = \vec{M} \times \vec{B}
= 0.1(-\hat{i}) \times (2\times 10^{-3} \hat{j})
= (0.1 \times 2\times 10^{-3}) (-\hat{i} \times \hat{j})
Using the cross product rule, \(-\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = -\hat{k}\).
\vec{\tau} = 2\times 10^{-4} (-\hat{k}) \text{ N} \cdot \text{m}
The magnitude of the torque is \(2\times 10^{-4}\) N-m and its direction is along the negative Z-direction.

The deflection in moving coil galvanometer falls from 25 divisions to 5 division when a shunt of 24Ω is applied. The resistance of galvanometer coil will be :
questions.explanation:
In a moving coil galvanometer, the current is proportional to the deflection.
i \propto \theta
Let \(i\) be the total current and \(i_{g}\) be the current through the galvanometer after the shunt is applied. The deflection is proportional to the current flowing through the galvanometer. Initially, the current for 25 divisions is \(i\). After shunting, the current for 5 divisions is \(i_{g}\).
\frac{i_{g}}{i} = \frac{5}{25}
5i_{g} = i
The potential difference is the same across the galvanometer and the shunt resistor.
Let G be the resistance of the galvanometer and S be the resistance of the shunt.
S(i - i_{g}) = i_{g} G
Substitute \(i = 5i_{g}\) and \(S = 24 \Omega\) into the equation:
24 (5i_{g} - i_{g}) = i_{g} G
24 \times 4 i_{g} = i_{g} G
Canceling \(i_{g}\) from both sides:
G = 24 \times 4 = 96
Therefore, the resistance of the galvanometer coil is 96 Ω.

questions.question: A rigid wire consists of a semicircular portion of radius R and two straight sections. The wire is partially immersed in a perpendicular magnetic field \(B = B_{0}\hat{j}\) as shown in figure. The magnetic force on the wire if it has a current \(i\) is :
questions.explanation:
### Solution

The magnetic force on a current-carrying wire in a uniform magnetic field is given by \(\vec{F} = i(\vec{L}_{eff} \times \vec{B})\), where \(\vec{L}_{eff}\) is the effective length vector from the start to the end point of the wire segment.
From the diagram, the semicircular wire segment effectively connects two points along the x-axis. If the current flows from \((-R, 0)\) to \((R, 0)\) through the semicircle, the effective length vector is \(\vec{L}_{eff} = 2R\hat{i}\).
There is a discrepancy between the problem statement and the diagram regarding the direction of the magnetic field.

### Case 1: According to the question statement

If \(\vec{B} = B_{0}\hat{j}\) (as stated in the question):
\vec{F} = i(2R\hat{i}) \times (B_{0}\hat{j})
\vec{F} = 2iRB_{0}(\hat{i} \times \hat{j})
\vec{F} = 2iRB_{0}\hat{k}
This result \(2iRB_{0}\hat{k}\) does not match any of the given options.

### Case 2: According to the diagram

The diagram shows the magnetic field as circles with dots, which indicates that the magnetic field is directed out of the page, i.e., in the \(+\hat{k}\) direction. So, if \(\vec{B} = B_{0}\hat{k}\) (according to the diagram):
\vec{F} = i(2R\hat{i}) \times (B_{0}\hat{k})
\vec{F} = 2iRB_{0}(\hat{i} \times \hat{k})
\vec{F} = 2iRB_{0}(-\hat{j})
\vec{F} = -2iRB_{0}\hat{j}
This result \(-2iRB_{0}\hat{j}\) matches option (1).
Therefore, considering the magnetic field direction as depicted in the diagram, the magnetic force on the wire is \(-2iRB_{0}\hat{j}\).

questions.question:
An electron is moving along the positive x-axis. If the uniform magnetic field is applied parallel to the negative z-axis, then
• A. The electron will experience magnetic force along positive y-axis
• B. The electron will experience magnetic force along negative y-axis
• C. The electron will not experience any force in magnetic field
• D. The electron will continue to move along the positive x-axis
• E. The electron will move along circular path in magnetic field
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Identify the given vectors

The electron is moving along the positive x-axis, so its velocity vector is \(\vec{V} = V \hat{i}\).
The uniform magnetic field is applied parallel to the negative z-axis, so the magnetic field vector is \(\vec{B} = -B \hat{k}\).
The charge of an electron is \(q = -e\).

### Step 2: Calculate the magnetic force

The magnetic force \(\vec{F}\) on a charged particle is given by the Lorentz force law:
\vec{F} = q(\vec{V} \times \vec{B})
Substitute the values for the electron:
\vec{F} = -e(V \hat{i} \times (-B \hat{k}))
\vec{F} = -e(-VB (\hat{i} \times \hat{k}))
Using the cross product rule, \(\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}\).
\vec{F} = -e(-VB(-\hat{j}))
\vec{F} = -e(VB\hat{j})
\vec{F} = -eVB\hat{j}
This result indicates that the magnetic force on the electron is directed along the negative y-axis. Therefore, statement B is correct.

### Step 3: Determine the path of the electron

Since the magnetic force \(\vec{F}\) is always perpendicular to the velocity \(\vec{V}\) (i.e., \(\vec{F} \perp \vec{V}\)), the force does no work on the electron. This means the speed of the electron remains constant, but its direction changes continuously. The magnetic force acts as a centripetal force, causing the electron to move in a circular path. Therefore, statement E is correct.

### Step 4: Choose the correct option

Based on our analysis, statements B and E are correct. The option that includes both B and E is (1).

questions.question: A moving coil galvanometer has 50 turns and each turn has an area \(2 \times 10^{-4}\) \(\text{m}^2\). The magnetic field produced by the magnet inside the galvanometer is \(0.02\text{T}\). The torsional constant of the suspension wire is \(10^{-4}\) \(\text{Nm rad}^{-1}\). When a current flows through the galvanometer, a full scale deflection occurs if the coil rotates by \(0.2\) \(\text{rad}\). The resistance of the coil of the galvanometer is \(50\Omega\). This galvanometer is to be converted into an ammeter capable of measuring current in the range \(0 - 1.0\text{A}\). For this purpose, a shunt resistance is to be added in parallel to the galvanometer. The value of this shunt resistance, in ohms, is _______.
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Given values are:
N = 50
A = 2 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{m}^2
C = 10^{-4} \, \text{Nm rad}^{-1}
R = 50 \, \Omega
B = 0.02 \, \text{T}
\theta = 0.2 \, \text{rad}
For full scale deflection, the torque on the coil is balanced by the restoring torque of the suspension wire:
Ni_{g}AB = C\theta
From this, we can find the galvanometer current \(i_{g}\):
i_{g} = \frac{C\theta}{NAB}
i_{g} = \frac{10^{-4} \times 0.2}{50 \times 2 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.02}
i_{g} = 0.1 \, \text{A}
To convert the galvanometer into an ammeter with a range of \(0 - 1.0\text{A}\), a shunt resistance \(S\) is connected in parallel. The total current \(i = 1.0\text{A}\). The current through the galvanometer is \(i_{g}\) and the current through the shunt is \(i - i_{g}\). Since the galvanometer and shunt are in parallel, the voltage across them is the same:
i_{g} \times R = (i - i_{g}) S
0.1 \times 50 = (1 - 0.1) S
5 = 0.9 S
Solving for \(S\):
S = \frac{5}{0.9} = \frac{50}{9} \, \Omega
S \approx 5.555 \, \Omega

questions.question: In a vacuum chamber, a particle of charge \(1 \mu C\) and mass \(1 mg\) is projected with a velocity \((\hat{i}+2\hat{j})\) \(ms^{-1}\) from the XZ plane at time \(t = 0\) in an electric field of \(1\hat{i}\) \(Vm^{-1}\). At \(t = 0.2 s\), the electric field is switched off and a magnetic field of \(6\hat{j}\) \(T\) is switched on. The acceleration due to gravity is \(-10\hat{j}\) \(ms^{-2}\). Correct option(s) is/are:
options: The vertical distance of the particle from the XZ plane at \(t = 0.3 s\) is \(15 cm\).
The vertical distance of the particle from the XZ plane at \(t = 0.4 s\) is \(10 cm\).
The radius of the trajectory of the particle for \(t > 0.2 s\) is \(20 cm\).
The particle will be in the XZ plane at \(t = 0.35 s\).
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution


### Step 1: Identify given data and initial conditions

Given:
m = 1mg = 1 \times 10^{-6} kg
q = 1 \times 10^{-6} C
\vec{v}_{0} = (\hat{i}+2\hat{j})m/s
Initial position: XZ plane, so \(y_{0} = 0\).

### Step 2: Analyze motion from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 0.2 s\)

During this period, an electric field \(\vec{E} = 1\hat{i}\) \(Vm^{-1}\) and gravity \(\vec{g} = -10\hat{j}\) \(m/s^2\) are present.
The acceleration \(\vec{a}_{1}\) is given by:
\vec{a}_{1} = \frac{q\vec{E}}{m} + \vec{g} = \frac{(1 \times 10^{-6} C)(1\hat{i} Vm^{-1})}{1 \times 10^{-6} kg} + (-10\hat{j} m/s^2)
\vec{a}_{1} = (1\hat{i} - 10\hat{j}) m/s^2
Velocity at \(t = 0.2 s\):
\vec{V}_{(0.2)} = \vec{v}_{0} + \vec{a}_{1}t = (\hat{i}+2\hat{j}) + (\hat{i}-10\hat{j})(0.2)
\vec{V}_{(0.2)} = \hat{i}+2\hat{j} + 0.2\hat{i}-2\hat{j} = 1.2\hat{i} m/s
y-position at \(t = 0.2 s\):
s_{y} = u_{y}t + \frac{1}{2} a_{y} t^2
y(0.2) - y(0) = (2)(0.2) + \frac{1}{2}(-10)(0.2)^2
y(0.2) - 0 = 0.4 - 5(0.04) = 0.4 - 0.2 = 0.2 m
y(0.2) = 0.2 m = 20 cm

### Step 3: Analyze motion for \(t > 0.2 s\)

After \(t = 0.2 s\), the electric field is switched off, and a magnetic field \(\vec{B}=(6\hat{j})T\) is switched on. Gravity \(\vec{g}=-10\hat{j}\) \(m/s^2\) is still present.
The new initial velocity for this phase is \(\vec{v}_{1} = 1.2\hat{i}\) \(m/s\) (which is \(\vec{V}_{(0.2)}\)).
Acceleration due to magnetic force \(\vec{a}_{B}\):
\vec{a}_{B} = \frac{\vec{F}_{B}}{m} = \frac{q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})}{m}
\vec{a}_{B} = \frac{(1 \times 10^{-6} C)}{1 \times 10^{-6} kg} [1.2\hat{i} \times 6\hat{j}] = 1 [7.2 (\hat{i} \times \hat{j})]
\vec{a}_{B} = 7.2\hat{k} m/s^2
The magnetic force causes circular motion in the XZ plane (since \(\vec{v}\) is along x-axis and \(\vec{B}\) is along y-axis, \(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}\) is along z-axis). It does not affect the y-component of velocity. The y-component of motion is only affected by gravity.
Let \(\tau = t - 0.2\) be the time elapsed since \(t = 0.2 s\).
The initial y-velocity at \(\tau = 0\) (i.e., \(t = 0.2 s\)) is \(u_{y} = 0\) (since \(\vec{V}_{(0.2)} = 1.2\hat{i}\)).
The y-position relative to \(y(0.2)\) is:
s_{y} = u_{y} \tau + \frac{1}{2} a_{y} \tau^2 = 0 \cdot \tau + \frac{1}{2}(-10)\tau^2 = -5\tau^2
The absolute y-position at time \(t\) (for \(t > 0.2 s\)) is:
y(t) = y(0.2) + s_{y} = 0.2 - 5\tau^2
y(t) = 0.2 - 5(t - 0.2)^2

### Step 4: Evaluate options

(A) The vertical distance of the particle from the XZ plane at \(t = 0.3 s\):
y(0.3) = 0.2 - 5(0.3 - 0.2)^2 = 0.2 - 5(0.1)^2 = 0.2 - 5(0.01) = 0.2 - 0.05 = 0.15 m = 15 cm
Option (A) is correct.
(B) The vertical distance of the particle from the XZ plane at \(t = 0.4 s\):
y(0.4) = 0.2 - 5(0.4 - 0.2)^2 = 0.2 - 5(0.2)^2 = 0.2 - 5(0.04) = 0.2 - 0.2 = 0 m
Option (B) is incorrect (it's 0 cm, not 10 cm).
(C) The radius of the trajectory of the particle for \(t > 0.2 s\):
The radius of the circular path due to magnetic force is \(R = \frac{mv_{\perp}}{qB}\).
Here, \(v_{\perp}\) is the component of velocity perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\). At \(t = 0.2 s\), \(\vec{v} = 1.2\hat{i}\) and \(\vec{B} = 6\hat{j}\). So, \(v_{\perp} = 1.2 m/s\).
R = \frac{(1 \times 10^{-6} kg)(1.2 m/s)}{(1 \times 10^{-6} C)(6 T)} = \frac{1.2}{6} = 0.2 m = 20 cm
Option (C) is correct.
(D) The particle will be in the XZ plane when \(y(t) = 0\):
0.2 - 5(t - 0.2)^2 = 0
5(t - 0.2)^2 = 0.2
(t - 0.2)^2 = \frac{0.2}{5} = 0.04
t - 0.2 = \pm \sqrt{0.04} = \pm 0.2
t = 0.2 + 0.2 = 0.4 s \text{ or } t = 0.2 - 0.2 = 0 s
The particle is in the XZ plane at \(t = 0 s\) and \(t = 0.4 s\), not \(t = 0.35 s\).
Option (D) is incorrect.

Calculations: A face-centred cubic (F.C.C.) lattice has atoms of pure substance at the corner of the unit cell and/or atom each at the centre of the face of the unit cell.

questions.question:
A positive, singly ionized atom of mass number \(A_M\) is accelerated from rest by the voltage 192 V. Thereafter, it enters a rectangular region of width \(w\) with magnetic field \(\vec{B}_0 = 0.1\hat{k}\) Tesla, as shown in the figure. The ion finally hits a detector at the distance \(x\) below its starting trajectory.
[Given: Mass of neutron/proton = \((5/3) \times 10^{-27}\) kg, charge of the electron = \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C.]
Which of the following option(s) is(are) correct?
options: The value of \(x\) for \(H^+\) ion is 4 cm.
The value of \(x\) for an ion with \(A_M = 144\) is 48 cm.
For detecting ions with \(1 \le A_M \le 196\), the minimum height \((x_1 - x_0)\) of the detector is 55 cm.
The minimum width \(w\) of the region of the magnetic field for detecting ions with \(A_M = 196\) is 56 cm.
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Derive the expression for x

From the diagram, the distance \(x\) is twice the radius of the circular path \(R\) in the magnetic field.
x = 2R
The radius of the path is given by \(R = \frac{mv}{qB}\). So,
x = 2\frac{mv}{qB}
The kinetic energy gained by the ion after acceleration by voltage \(\Delta V\) is \(q\Delta V = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\). From this, the velocity \(v = \sqrt{\frac{2q\Delta V}{m}}\). Substituting this into the expression for \(x\):
x = 2\frac{m}{qB}\sqrt{\frac{2q\Delta V}{m}} = \frac{2}{B}\sqrt{\frac{2m\Delta V}{q}}
Given values: \(B = 0.1\) T, \(\Delta V = 192\) V, \(q = e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C. Mass of proton/neutron \(m_p = (5/3) \times 10^{-27}\) kg.

### Step 2: Calculate x for \(H^+\) ion (Option A)

For \(H^+\) ion, \(A_M = 1\), so \(m = 1 \times m_p = (5/3) \times 10^{-27}\) kg.
x = \frac{2}{0.1}\sqrt{\frac{2 \times (5/3) \times 10^{-27} \times 192}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}}
x \approx 3.91 \text{ cm}
Approximating to the nearest integer, \(x \approx 4\) cm. (A is correct)

### Step 3: Calculate x for an ion with \(A_M = 144\) (Option B)

From the formula \(x = \frac{2}{B}\sqrt{\frac{2m\Delta V}{q}}\), we see that \(x \propto \sqrt{m}\). Since \(m = A_M m_p\), we have \(x \propto \sqrt{A_M}\).
For \(H^+\), \(A_M = 1\). For the new ion, \(A_M = 144\).
\frac{x_{144}}{x_{H^+}} = \sqrt{\frac{144}{1}} = 12
x_{144} = 12 \times x_{H^+} = 12 \times 4 \text{ cm} = 48 \text{ cm}
(B is correct)

### Step 4: Calculate minimum height of detector \((x_1 - x_0)_{\min}\) for \(1 \le A_M \le 196\) (Option C)

The detector needs to cover the range of \(x\) values. The minimum value of \(x\) corresponds to \(A_M = 1\) (i.e., \(x_0 = x_{H^+}\)) and the maximum value of \(x\) corresponds to \(A_M = 196\) (i.e., \(x_1 = x_{196}\)).
We know \(x \propto \sqrt{A_M}\). So, \(x_{196} = x_{H^+} \sqrt{196} = 4 \text{ cm} \times 14 = 56\) cm.
The minimum height of the detector is \(x_1 - x_0 = x_{196} - x_{H^+}\).
(x_1 - x_0)_{\min} = 56 \text{ cm} - 4 \text{ cm} = 52 \text{ cm}
The option states 55 cm. (C is incorrect)

### Step 5: Calculate minimum width \(w_{\min}\) for \(A_M = 196\) (Option D)

The minimum width \(w\) of the magnetic field region must be at least the radius \(R\) of the path for the ion to complete its semi-circular trajectory and hit the detector. For the largest \(A_M\) (196), the radius will be largest.
w_{\min} = R_{196}
Since \(x = 2R\), then \(R = x/2\).
R_{196} = \frac{x_{196}}{2} = \frac{56 \text{ cm}}{2} = 28 \text{ cm}
The option states 56 cm. (D is incorrect)

questions.question: A circular coil of radius R and N turns has negligible resistance. As shown in the schematic figure, its two ends are connected to two wires and it is hanging by those wires with its plane being vertical. The wires are connected to a capacitor with charge Q through a switch. The coil is in a horizontal uniform magnetic field \(B_{0}\) parallel to the plane of the coil. When the switch is closed, the capacitor gets discharged through the coil in a very short time. By the time the capacitor is discharged fully, magnitude of the angular momentum gained by the coil will be (assume that the discharge time is so short that the coil has hardly rotated during this time)-
questions.explanation:
Torque experienced by circular loop = \(\vec{M} \times \vec{B}\)
where \(\vec{M}\) is magnetic moment
\(\vec{B}\) is magnetic field
\(\therefore \tau = i\pi R^{2} N B_{0}\) [at the instant shown \(\theta = \pi/2\)]
\(\therefore \vec{\tau} dt = d\vec{L} = i\pi R^{2} N B_{0} dt\)
Integrating both sides over the discharge time:
\int d\vec{L} = \int i\pi R^{2} N B_{0} dt
\Delta L = \pi R^{2} N B_{0} \int i dt
Since the capacitor discharges fully, the total charge passed through the coil is Q.
\int i dt = Q
Therefore, the magnitude of the angular momentum gained by the coil is:
\Delta L = Q\pi R^{2} N B_{0}
The final answer is \(\pi NQB_{0}R^{2}\).

questions.question: A thin stiff insulated metal wire is bent into a circular loop with its two ends extending tangentially from the same point of the loop. The wire loop has mass \(m\) and radius \(r\) and it is in a uniform vertical magnetic field \(B_0\), as shown in the figure. Initially, it hangs vertically downwards, because of acceleration due to gravity \(g\), on two conducting supports at \(P\) and \(Q\). When a current \(I\) is passed through the loop, the loop turns about the line \(PQ\) by an angle \(\theta\) given by
questions.explanation:
### Solution

For equilibrium, the torque due to gravity must balance the torque due to the magnetic field.

### Torque due to gravity

The center of mass of the loop is at a distance \(r\) from the line \(PQ\). When the loop turns by an angle \(\theta\), the vertical displacement of the center of mass creates a restoring torque.
\tau_{\text{gravity}} = mgr \sin\theta

### Torque due to magnetic field

The magnetic moment of the loop is \(M = I A = I (\pi r^2)\). The torque due to the magnetic field is given by \(\vec{\tau}_{\text{magnetic}} = \vec{M} \times \vec{B_0}\). From the diagram, the angle between the magnetic moment vector \(\vec{M}\) (which is perpendicular to the plane of the loop) and the magnetic field \(\vec{B_0}\) (which is vertical) is \((90^\circ - \theta)\).
\tau_{\text{magnetic}} = M B_0 \sin(90^\circ - \theta) = M B_0 \cos\theta
\tau_{\text{magnetic}} = (I \pi r^2) B_0 \cos\theta

### Equilibrium condition

At equilibrium, the gravitational torque balances the magnetic torque:
\tau_{\text{gravity}} = \tau_{\text{magnetic}}
mgr \sin\theta = I \pi r^2 B_0 \cos\theta
\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \frac{I \pi r^2 B_0}{mgr}
\tan\theta = \frac{I \pi r B_0}{mg}
The correct option is (A).

questions.question: A conducting solid sphere of radius \(R\) and mass \(M\) carries a charge \(Q\). The sphere is rotating about an axis passing through its center with a uniform angular speed \(\omega\). The ratio of the magnitudes of the magnetic dipole moment to the angular momentum about the same axis is given as \(\alpha \frac{Q}{2M}\). The value of \(\alpha\) is ______.
questions.explanation:
dM = dIA
A = \pi r^2 = \pi(R \sin \theta)^2
dI = \frac{da}{T} = \frac{\sigma(2\pi r)(Rd\theta)\omega}{2\pi}
dI = \frac{\sigma 2\pi R^2 \omega \sin \theta d\theta}{2\pi}
dI = \sigma R^2 \omega \sin \theta d\theta

### Magnetic dipole moment :

M = \int dM = \int_{0}^{\pi} \sigma R^2 \omega \pi R^2 \sin^3 \theta d\theta
M = \sigma R^4 \omega \pi \int_{0}^{\pi} \sin^3 \theta d\theta \quad \left( \because \int_{0}^{\pi} \sin^3 \theta d\theta = \frac{4}{3} \right)
M = \left(\frac{Q}{4\pi R^2}\right) R^4 \omega \pi \left(\frac{4}{3}\right)

### Magnetic dipole moment

M = \frac{QR^2\omega}{3}

### Angular momentum

L = \left(\frac{2}{5}MR^2\right)\omega
\frac{M}{L} = \frac{QR^2\omega}{3 \times \frac{2}{5}MR^2\omega} = \frac{Q}{2M}\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)
\alpha = \frac{5}{3} = 1.67
